conflicts: Edition and date of the text this project relies on. Nov. 9, 1886.]' and it prints press notices and correspondence through late 1886. The Internet Archive scan it derives from (onehundredproofs00carp) is catalogued 1886. Baird of the Smithsonian dated 6 January 1886, reads 'deposited in Library of Congress October 8, 1884' with a bracketed '[1885]' inserted. The figure rests on an editorial correction of the printed source and should be labelled as such.

A sixth edition is not evidenced in this copy. Carpenter separately claimed to Schadewald's sources that he had disposed of nearly 12,000 copies.

Date of the 'Common Sense' astronomy work. The 1885 title page reads "Author of 'Common Sense' on Astronomy, (London, 1866;)". Wikipedia gives Theoretical Astronomy Examined and Exposed, 1864. Title and date of Carpenter's Bedford Canal book. Schadewald gives 'Water, Not Convex: The Earth Not a Globe!' (1871), and the 1885 title page lists 'Wallace's Wonderful Water' (Schadewald: 1875). Wikipedia gives 'The Bedford Level Experiment' (1872). Not resolved here; none of these texts was reached.

The movement's memorial notice for its founder, written by the man who knew him personally, is wrong about his age by twenty-one years — whether through Carpenter or his compositor cannot be told from this file. It is a small illustration of the standing rule that the movement's internal genealogy is evidence of what the movement says about itself and nothing more.

PER-PTOLEMY.name: Claudius Ptolemy
conflicts: DATES. Our record's 'c. 100 – c. 170 CE' matches Wikipedia; MacTutor (St Andrews) gives 'c. 85 – c. 165'. Neither is anchored — no ancient source records his birth or death. The only firm anchors are his own dated observations (26 March 127 to 2 February 141) and the Canobic Inscription of 146/147. Nothing in this biography turns on the difference. Recommendation: keep the existing range and print the observation window alongside it, which is what the `dates` field above does. Reported, not silently resolved.

THE FABRICATION CHARGE — LIVE, AND WE DO NOT SETTLE IT. R. R. Newton, 'The Crime of Claudius Ptolemy' (1977), argued that observations were computed from theory and then reported as observed, calling him 'the most successful fraud in the history of science.' Owen Gingerich rejected the fraud characterisation; Gerd Graßhoff argues he was selecting among measurements without any modern statistical apparatus for doing so; and the 2022 multispectral recovery of Hipparchan star coordinates from the Codex Climaci Rescriptus (Gysembergh, Williams & Zingg, JHA 53:4) shows Ptolemy's catalogue was not simply copied from Hipparchus — while also suggesting Hipparchus's own coordinates may have been the more accurate. The dispute is unresolved and this record takes no side. It is also orthogonal to the finding here: what the list does with the Almagest is unaffected by whether its author padded his data.

REALIST OR INSTRUMENTALIST. Duhem's 'save the phenomena' reading has Ptolemy agnostic about whether his circles are physically real, and it is that Ptolemy the modern movement borrows. Against it: the Planetary Hypotheses assigns physical distances in Earth radii and nests the spheres so that they touch, which reads as a physical cosmos rather than a calculating device (see Murschel, JHA 26 (1995), 33). Live scholarly dispute, reported not adjudicated. It matters here only in one direction — on either reading the Earth in the middle is a sphere.

WHETHER 'PTOLEMY PREDICTED ECLIPSES FOR 600 YEARS' IS TRUE AT ALL. Both movement texts assert it, and Rowbotham's own source is a Victorian popular history (Smith, 'Rise and Progress of Astronomy'), quoted at second hand. We have not traced the 600-year figure to anything in the Almagest or the Handy Tables, and we do not assert it is false — only that the movement's Ptolemy arrives through nineteenth-century popularisation and not through the text.
